blocks.text: I taught a 4B model to talk like a pirate on my DGX Spark. Here's everything I had to learn to get there.
For three months there was a note in my obsidian vault called "TODO - Finish Unsloth Setup on Spark".
Last night I finally did it. 743 training examples, 7 minutes 20 seconds of training, and out came a 4B model that answers every question like a pirate captain 🏴‍☠️.
No system prompt, no "talk like a pirate, make no mistakes". It's embedded in the weights now!

But it wasn't as simple as I thought. Here's what actually happened: the first time I read an Unsloth tutorial, I understood maybe half the words in it. The tutorials are full of words like LoRA, rank, alpha, tokenizer, chat template, gradient accumulation, train on completions... The list goes on and on.
Every tutorial assumes you already know what they all mean, and none of them tell you which ones actually matter.

So this is the article I wish I'd read first to help me understand things better. Every concept in plain words, in the order you'll hit them, with the real numbers from my experience and the things that broke along the way.
First: what fine-tuning actually is
A model like Qwen3-4B goes through two big stages before you ever touch it.

Pretraining is where it reads a huge chunk of the internet and learns to predict the next word. That's where the knowledge comes from: facts, grammar, code, how arguments are built. It costs millions of dollars and you're not doing it at home.

Instruction tuning is where the lab teaches that raw text predictor to behave like an assistant: answer the question, follow instructions, stop when it's done. That's the "Instruct" in Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507.

Fine-tuning is you taking that finished model and nudging it further with your own examples so it fits your specific needs. And here's the part nobody says out loud: fine-tuning is bad at teaching new facts and great at teaching behavior. Tone, format, habits, a persona, when to reach for a tool. You're not filling it with knowledge, you're coaching how it uses what it already has.
Keep that in mind. It explains why my first run taught the model absolutely nothing.
Installing it on a Spark

You get two things with that command: the unsloth command-line tool (train, chat, inference, export) and Unsloth Studio, a web UI on localhost:8888 if you'd rather click. I use the cli as I use my sparks as dedicated inference machines and I just ssh into them.
Run #1: the smoke test that taught nothing
Every Unsloth tutorial starts the same way: a small model, FineTome-100k (a public dataset of 100,000 generic question-and-answer conversations), 60 training steps.
So I did that.
Two lessons here, one annoying and one important.

The annoying one: my first attempt died with path escapes root, cuz I passed a full path like --output-dir /home/jvr0x/tmp/..., and the CLI only accepts output folders inside ~/.unsloth/studio/outputs.
Lesson: Pass a plain name and it lands there. Want it somewhere else? Symlink it afterwards.

The important one: it trained fine (173 seconds) and changed basically nothing. 60 steps × 8 examples per step = 480 examples out of 100,000. And even the full dataset wouldn't have helped much, because FineTome is generic Q&A, exactly the kind of thing an Instruct model already does well. You can't teach a model something it already knows.

So the real rule of fine-tuning: pick data that makes the model do something it doesn't do today, and something you can check at a glance. That's why pirate. It's useless in practice, and that's the point. When you're learning, you want a result where "did it work?" takes one second to answer.
The dataset: a big model teaches a small one
I don't have 743 pirate conversations lying around. But I do have a box that serves big models.
So I used two. The teacher was the legendary Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (NVFP4), served locally through lmswitch, my model switcher. The student was Qwen3-4B, the one that actually gets trained.
A ~120-line Python script pulls prompts from FineTome, sends each one to the teacher with this system prompt:
You are a salty old pirate captain. Answer every request fully and correctly, but always speak in heavy pirate dialect [...] Facts, math and code must stay correct.
...and saves the teacher's answer without the system prompt. That's the trick. The student sees a normal question paired with a pirate answer, hundreds of times, until pirate is just how it talks 😈.
This is called distillation (a big model's behavior copied into a small one), and this specific flavor, where you bake a system prompt into the weights, is called context distillation.
A few details that matter more than they look:
20 prompts held out. They never go into training. Testing a model on questions it trained on is like grading a student on the homework they copied.
10% of rows get a generic system prompt ("You are a helpful assistant."). Otherwise the model could learn "no system prompt = pirate" and drop the act the moment an app sends one.

743, not 800. I asked for 800. A few teacher answers hit the length cap and got dropped, a couple of requests came back HTTP 500, and the script ran out of spare prompts. So I did 743, it was good enough for the first trial.
Generation took about 10~15 min, I didn't really checked. Each training example is one line of JSON (the format's called JSONL), and the very first one in my file looks like this:

A fun detail I only caught while writing this: the regex in that answer is correct, but the teacher's example comment says the sample string has 7 words. It has 8. Whatever the teacher gets wrong, the student learns too!
Your student can only be as good as your teacher's data, so read some of it before you train on it.
The tokenizer: models don't read words
Now the concepts that sound alien. Start here, because everything else builds on it.

Models don't see letters or words. They see tokens: chunks of text, each mapped to a number. A short common word is usually one token, a long or rare word gets split into pieces, and spaces and punctuation get tokens too. The tokenizer is the lookup table that turns text into those numbers and back.
Two things follow from that:

Every model family has its own tokenizer, and you can't mix them. Qwen's token #1000 isn't Llama's token #1000. That's why your fine-tune's output folder ships a copy of the tokenizer (an 11 MB tokenizer.json) right next to the trained weights.
Lengths are measured in tokens, not words. --max-seq-length 2048 means any conversation longer than 2048 tokens gets cut off. My whole run pushed 678,785 tokens through the model.
The chat template: the part that silently breaks everything
This is the one I'd have gotten wrong on my own.

When you chat with a model, you think in messages: system, user, assistant. The model doesn't. It sees one long string of tokens, and the "roles" are just special marker tokens inside that string. Qwen uses a format called ChatML, so the one-line test row I used to dry-run my config actually looks like this to the model:
That's the chat template: the recipe that turns a list of messages into the exact string the model was trained on. Llama, Gemma, Mistral, they all use different markers.

Why it matters: train with one template and serve with another, and the model sees markers it never learned. Best case it gets dumber. Worst case it never stops talking, because <|im_end|> is literally how it learned to say "I'm done."

Good news is that Unsloth handles this for you (the log says Applying Unsloth chat template: qwen3-instruct), and the template travels with the model when you export it. Your job is to not override it with a different one when you serve it.
Train on completions: only grade the answers

Each example has a question and an answer. By default, training teaches the model to predict every token in the example, the question included. That's wasted effort. I don't need the model to get better at writing questions about regex.
train_on_completions: true masks the question out, so the model only gets graded on the assistant's answer. For a persona, that's exactly what you want.
Gotcha: there's no CLI flag for it. It only exists in the YAML config file.
LoRA: training a model without touching the model
Qwen3-4B is about 4 billion numbers (called weights, or parameters). Full fine-tuning updates all 4 billion. That needs a lot of memory, and it risks wrecking things the model already does well.

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes those 4 billion weights completely. It bolts small extra matrices, called adapters, onto specific spots inside the model and trains only those. At the end you get the original model untouched, plus a small file of corrections that sits on top of it.
Think of it as a clip-on lens instead of regrinding the camera's own lens.
The knobs:

Target modules: where the adapters go. Each of Qwen3-4B's 36 layers has attention parts (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, roughly "what should I pay attention to") and feed-forward parts (gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj, roughly "what do I do with it"). I targeted all seven, which is the standard choice.
Rank (r): how big each adapter is, basically how much it can learn. I used r=16. Higher rank, more capacity, more memory. 16 is plenty for a speaking style.
Alpha: a volume knob for how loudly the adapter speaks over the frozen model. The effective strength is alpha divided by rank, so alpha=16 with r=16 gives 1, a neutral setting.
The result: 33 million trainable numbers against the model's ~4 billion. Under 1%. The entire pirate personality is a 126 MB file.

QLoRA is the same idea, except the frozen base gets loaded in 4-bit (--load-in-4bit) to save memory, while the adapters still train in full precision. A 4B model on a 128 GB Spark doesn't need it. But it's the default, and it's what lets you fine-tune much bigger models on the same box later.
The training knobs, in plain words
Here's the whole config:
Epochs: 2. The model reads the whole dataset twice.

Batch size 2 × gradient accumulation 4 = 8. The GPU looks at 2 examples, remembers what it learned, repeats that 4 times, and only then updates the weights. It behaves like a batch of 8 without needing the memory for 8 at once.
Steps: 186. 743 examples / 8 per step ≈ 93 steps per epoch, × 2 epochs. A step is one weight update.
Learning rate: 2e-4. How big each correction is. Too high and training goes unstable, too low and nothing moves. 2e-4 is the standard LoRA starting point.

One Spark-specific warning: turn off anything else hogging memory before you train. The GPU and the system share the same 128 GB, and I had to redo the process cuz I had GLM 5.3 Flash running taking almost all my memory available. Teacher off, then train.
The scoreboard
Training time: 7 minutes 20 seconds
Tokens processed: 678,785, at ~1,540 tokens/s on the GB10
Loss: 2.14 on the first step, 0.81 averaged over the last 10
Output: a 126 MB LoRA adapter 🌟

Loss is the number you watch while training runs. Roughly: how surprised the model is by the correct next token. It starts high because the model expects "Sure! Here's how to..." and keeps getting "Arr, ye scallywag...". It drops as the model learns to expect pirate.

And here's the uncomfortable truth: loss going down doesn't mean the model got smarter. It means it got better at predicting this data. Mine learned a dialect. It didn't learn a single new fact, and with 743 examples it shouldn't. Low loss tells you training worked, not that the model is good. You still have to test it!!
Testing it: same question, both models
The test is simple. Take the held-out prompts, ask the original Qwen3-4B and the fine-tune the exact same question, compare.
--top-k 1 makes the model always pick its single most likely next token. No dice rolls. So any difference between the two answers comes from the training, not from randomness.
Result: the original answers like a normal assistant. The fine-tune answers the same question in pirate, without being asked to 🔥
Two dumb things happened on the way, and I'm including them cuz you'll hit them too:

My terminal ate a flag. I pasted the long test command and got 400: command not found. The terminal had wrapped the line and split --max-new-tokens from its 400. Put long commands in a script file and move on.

I got confused about which model I'd trained. The output said Qwen3-4B-Instruct and my first reaction was "wait, didn't we train the 35B?" No. The 35B only wrote the data. The 4B is the student. When you do distillation, write down which model is which, because you will mix them up if you do this like me late night doing this via Termius 😅.
Beyond the voice, check two things: are the facts and the math still right, and does it stop cleanly or ramble? A fine-tune that nails the style but breaks the answers is a failed fine-tune.
Export: from adapter to something you can serve
The adapter only works on top of the exact base model it was trained on. To serve it in llama.cpp, Ollama or LM Studio, you merge it into the base and export a single file:

Merge: the adapter's corrections get folded permanently into the weights. Here's a sneaky one: because of QLoRA, the adapter's config records its base as qwen3-4b-instruct-2507-unsloth-bnb-4bit, the 4-bit copy it trained against, not the model I named on the command line. --no-load-in-4bit makes the merge happen on the full-precision base instead, so you don't bake the 4-bit rounding into your final model.
GGUF: the file format llama.cpp and ollama use. Weights, tokenizer and chat template, all in one file.
Quantization, q8_0: stores each weight in 8 bits instead of 16. Roughly half the size, and at 8 bits it's close to lossless. Result: a 4.3 GB file, plus a ready-made Ollama Modelfile.
One gotcha: Unsloth names the GGUF after the base model (qwen3-4b-instruct-2507.Q8_0.gguf), not after your fine-tune. Rename it right away or you'll forget and mix them up later.

And here's the end result in case you are interested in talking to a pirate!👇 
https://huggingface.co/jvr0x/Qwen3-4B-Pirate-GGUF
The cheat sheet
The whole pipeline, once the words make sense:
Install: curl -fsSL https://unsloth.ai/install.sh | sh
Make data the model can't already produce. A bigger teacher model plus a system prompt works great. Hold out ~20 prompts.
Write a YAML config: LoRA r=16, alpha=16, train on completions, 2 epochs.
unsloth train -c train.yaml
A/B the base vs the fine-tune on the held-out prompts, with --top-k 1.
unsloth export ... -f gguf -q q8_0 --no-load-in-4bit, then rename the file.
What this isn't

A serious model. It's one 4B, 743 synthetic examples, and a style that's funny and totally useless, but it taught me the basics! I checked a handful of answers by eye, I didn't run a benchmark to measure whether talking like a pirate costs any accuracy. And the unsloth train CLI only does supervised fine-tuning, where the model learns from example answers. Reinforcement learning, where it learns from a score instead, needs a Python script. That's the next level up.

But it's the full loop, end to end, on one Spark: a big local model writes the data, a small one learns it, and the result gets exported to a file I can serve anywhere. No cloud, no API bill, and the training step takes almost no time.
Credit where it's due 🙏 the @UnslothAI team for turning this into a one-line install on ARM, and Maxime Labonne for FineTome-100k.
What's next
Here's why I actually care about any of this.
Back in July 2024, Andrej Karpathy posted this:
LLM model size competition is intensifying… backwards! My bet is that we'll see models that "think" very well and reliably that are very very small.
His argument: today's models are huge because we train them to memorize the internet, and in that data, thinking and knowledge come tangled together. So you need big models first, to untangle it:
the models have to first get larger before they can get smaller, because we need their (automated) help to refactor and mold the training data into ideal, synthetic formats.

He calls it a staircase: one model generating the training data for the next. And he says if you train a GPT-2-sized model (1.5B parameters) on that ideal dataset, "it will be a really strong / smart model by today's standards."
Read that again after this article 🔥 A big model writing the training data for a small one is exactly what I just did, at toy scale. The 35B was the top step, the 4B was the next one.

A year later he gave it a name, the "cognitive core": "a few billion param model that maximally sacrifices encyclopedic knowledge for capability." Reasoning with a dial. Aggressively tool-using. It doesn't know what date William the Conqueror's reign ended, but it can look it up. It even has on-device LoRA slots for personalization, the same adapters from this article. Then on Dwarkesh Patel's podcast he put a number on it:
I almost feel like we can get cognitive cores that are very good at even a billion parameters.
Because, in his words, most of what the giant models do "is memory work instead of cognitive work. But what we really want is the cognitive part, delete the memory."
So that's the project. I'm going to train my own ~1B model and teach it two things only: how to reason from first principles, and how to use tools properly.

No encyclopedia. The tools handle the facts. My bet: on real agentic work, where the job is to think, call the right tool and check the result, a 1B that does exactly that can go head-to-head with frontier models many times its size.

To be fair to @Karpathy: that last part is my bet, not his. He's said openly that the cognitive core will lack "top tier problem-solving capability" compared to the big cloud models, and he puts the really good version years out. He's probably right, but the tooling's here and I gotta try it out! Worst case scenario I learn a ton and publish every failed run 😄.

The plan: supervised fine-tuning on tool-calling traces from a big teacher first, then reinforcement learning where the reward is dead simple. Did the tool call work? Did the task get solved? Same Spark, all in public.
If you want the data-generation script or the exact config, drop me a line. And if you've tried teaching tool use to a small model, I'd love to hear what broke.
Cheers ✌️

data.markdown:
```yaml
model: unsloth/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507
data:
  local_dataset:
    - /home/<you>/finetune-pirate/data/train.jsonl
  format_type: chatml
training:
  training_type: lora
  max_seq_length: 2048
  load_in_4bit: true
  output_dir: qwen3-4b-pirate
  num_epochs: 2
  learning_rate: 2.0e-4
  batch_size: 2
  gradient_accumulation_steps: 4
  train_on_completions: true
lora:
  lora_r: 16
  lora_alpha: 16
```

```bash
unsloth train \
  --model unsloth/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 \
  --dataset mlabonne/FineTome-100k \
  --format-type chatml \
  --training-type lora \
  --max-seq-length 2048 \
  --load-in-4bit \
  --lora-r 16 --lora-alpha 16 \
  --num-epochs 1 --batch-size 2 \
  --gradient-accumulation-steps 4 \
  --learning-rate 2e-4 \
  --max-steps 60 \
  --output-dir finetune-qwen3-4b
```
